items.paragraph: Projects that recruit volunteers to count birds, record flowering dates or photograph insects are often dismissed by professional researchers on the grounds that amateurs make mistakes. The objection is true and largely beside the point. Individual records from volunteers are indeed less reliable than those of trained surveyors, but the errors tend to be random rather than systematic, and random errors shrink in importance as the number of observations grows. A thousand imperfect counts spread across a region can reveal a trend that a handful of expert surveys, confined to a few accessible sites, would miss altogether. The question to ask of citizen science is therefore not how careful each participant is but where and when the participants chose to look.

items.paragraph: It seems obvious that an operation cannot work by suggestion: the knife either repairs the tissue or it does not. The lesson is not that restriction was simply wrong, but that flexible visiting works when units plan for it rather than merely permit it.

items.paragraph: It is often assumed that digital records, because they can be copied without loss, are safer than paper ones. A manuscript can burn; a file can be duplicated a thousand times. Digital preservation is therefore less a matter of storing data than of continually maintaining the conditions under which data can be interpreted, a task that never finishes and is easy to neglect.

items.paragraph: Writing tools that suggest the next word or complete a sentence are usually judged by whether their suggestions are accurate, that is, whether they offer what the writer was about to type. By that standard they are improving quickly. But accuracy measured this way rewards the most probable continuation, and the most probable continuation is, by definition, the one that most writers have already used. A tool that is perfectly accurate in this sense would steer each writer a little towards the common phrase and away from the unusual one, and across millions of documents these small nudges could make prose more uniform without anyone deciding that it should be. The danger lies not in any single suggestion, which the writer is free to refuse, but in the cumulative pull of accepting the easy option many times a day.

items.paragraph: Radio drama is sometimes regarded as a poor relation of film and television, a form that lasted only until pictures could be added. Yet the absence of images is not simply a lack. Because the listener must supply faces, rooms and landscapes, each production is completed in a different imagination, and the scenes that would be most expensive or least convincing on screen, a battle at sea or a city on another planet, cost a radio producer little more than a few sounds and a sentence. What radio cannot do is control exactly what the audience sees, and so it suits stories that depend on voice, suggestion and inner life better than those that depend on precise visual spectacle. Its limitations and its strengths are, in large part, the same feature viewed from two sides.

items.paragraph: A census appears to be a passive instrument: the state asks who people are and writes down the answers. But the questions come first, and they are not neutral. To count people by language, religion or ethnicity, an official form must offer a fixed list of boxes, and those boxes rarely match the blurred, overlapping and shifting ways people actually describe themselves. Resources, representation and political claims come to be organised around them, and people begin to identify with the box that brings recognition. Counting, in short, can help to create the groups it claims merely to record. This does not mean censuses should stop asking such questions, since a state that refuses to count a disadvantaged group may also refuse to see its disadvantage; it means the categories deserve the scrutiny we give to any other policy choice.

items.paragraph: Style manuals routinely tell writers to avoid the passive voice, and the advice has hardened into a rule that many writers apply without thinking. The case against the passive is real but narrow. A passive sentence can hide the agent ('mistakes were made'), and a long run of passives can make prose feel inert. But the passive also does work that nothing else does as neatly. It lets a writer keep the topic of a paragraph in the subject position, so that a passage about a disease can go on talking about the disease ('it is spread by mosquitoes') rather than lurching to whatever happens to cause it. It lets scientists foreground a procedure rather than the person who carried it out, when the person is irrelevant. The useful question is never whether a sentence is passive but whether the reader needs to know who acted, and what the sentence should be about.

items.paragraph: Body mass index, a person's weight divided by the square of their height, is often attacked as a crude and misleading measure of health. The attack is fair when the number is applied to individuals without further thought: a muscular athlete can register as overweight, and the measure says nothing about where fat is carried, which matters for risk. But the index was never well suited to judging single bodies. Its strength lies in populations, where it is cheap, consistent and reasonably correlated with outcomes across large groups, making it useful for tracking trends over time. The fault lies less in the measure than in asking it to do a job, the assessment of one patient, for which other information is needed.

items.paragraph: Names for children rise and fall in popularity in waves that look remarkably like fashions in clothing, yet no industry advertises them and no designer sets the trend. (1) Parents usually want a name that sounds fresh without sounding strange, and they judge freshness largely by how rarely they have heard it among the children they know. (2) A name that is rising satisfies both demands at once, which is why more and more parents converge on it. (3) That very convergence destroys its appeal, since a name heard in every playground no longer sounds fresh to the next set of parents. The name then declines, and after two or three generations it begins to sound not dated but quaint, ready to be rediscovered. (4) In this way a trend can rise and fall without anyone directing it, driven only by many private choices that each respond to the choices of others.
